Keep the road clean. Mix with care.
fine: Xiong et al. 2020; Zhang & Sennrich 2019; Kim et al. 2025; Zhu et al. 2025 (Hyper-Connections);
Xie et al. 2025 (mHC, arXiv:2512.24880). The narration is a synthetic voice.

cap.n0: Every block of a language model has one express lane running past it.|What if you built four?
cap.n0b: And how would you keep four lanes from blowing up?
cap.n1: Start with one lane. A transformer is a tall stack of blocks:|attention, then a feed-forward layer,|again and again, dozens of times.
cap.n2: Each block doesn't replace its input. It adds a change on top:|x plus F of x. The plain x is an express road.|The block is a town you exit into,|and its result merges back onto the road.
cap.n3: Why does that matter?|Training sends a correction signal, the gradient,|backwards from the last layer to the first.|Her example:
cap.n4: The express road has no gates,|so the gradient rides straight down it.|ResNet made this shortcut the standard, about ten years ago.
cap.n5: Without it, the signal would pass through every block in turn,|like a message whispered down a long line of people.|By the end, it is mush.
cap.n6: The second thing a deep stack needs is normalization:|shift and scale a group of numbers,|so they average zero, with a standard spread.|But which group?
cap.n7: BatchNorm, from image models,|measures each feature across a whole batch of examples.|Like a tailor measuring the waist of everyone in a row.
cap.n8: LayerNorm measures one example at a time:|all the numbers of one token, head to toe.
cap.n9: Sentences come short and long, so batch averages wobble.|LayerNorm needs no batch at all.|And her slide is honest about the real reason:|experiments show it works better.
cap.n10: Modern models trim it further.|RMSNorm skips subtracting the average, and has no bias.|It only rescales.
cap.n11: In its 2019 paper, it matched LayerNorm's quality,|with 7 to 64 percent less running time,|depending on the model.|The Llama family uses it.
cap.n12: Now the real question.|Where on the highway do you put the toll gate?
cap.n13: The 2017 Transformer added first, then normalized.|That puts a gate right across the express road.|This is called Post-LN.
cap.n14: Every gradient has to squeeze through every gate.|In 2020, Xiong and colleagues showed|that Post-LN starts training with large gradients near the output,|so it needs a slow warm-up.
cap.n15: Pre-LN moves the gate onto the exit ramp.|Only the copy going into the block is normalized.|The road itself stays untouched.
cap.n16: Pre-LN can train without warm-up and reach comparable results.|BERT kept the original Post-LN.|GPT-2 moved the norm to the input. Her slide's verdict:|only earlier models, like BERT, used Post-LN.
cap.n17: Her point is that the names mislead.|What matters is not before or after.|It is whether a gate sits on the express road.
cap.n18: One more idea:|normalize what goes into the block,|and also what comes out, before it merges back.|Two gates, both on the ramp. The road stays clean.
cap.n19: This is Peri-LN. Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 do exactly this.|OLMo 2 uses a close cousin.|Models shipped it in 2024, and a paper studied it in 2025.
cap.n20: A norm is cheap next to the big matrix multiplications,|so an extra gate costs little.
cap.n21: So far, one road.|The residual shortcut itself had barely changed in ten years.|Then she asks:
cap.n22: Hyper-connections, from Zhu and colleagues in 2025,|copy the stream into several lanes, here four.|Each block reads a learned mix of the lanes,|and writes back into all of them.
cap.n23: The block itself still runs once,|so the expensive part costs the same.|Only the cheap merging gets richer.
cap.n24: But now the crossovers have weights. Her toy example:|if y is x1 plus x2, each input gets the full gradient back.
cap.n25: If y is 0.2 x1 plus 0.8 x2,|the gradients come back scaled, by 0.2 and by 0.8.|So the weights decide how much signal gets through.
cap.n26: Learned, they worked.|In the paper's big test, the model reached the baseline's loss|1.8 times faster, counted in training tokens.
cap.n27: Here is the catch. Those weights multiply,|layer after layer.|A weight of 1.1, a hundred times over, is about 13,800.|A weight of 0.9, a hundred times over,|is about 3 in 100,000.
cap.n28: A snowball, or a whisper.|When DeepSeek measured plain hyper-connections,|the signal gain through the stack hit about 3,000.
cap.n29: Their fix is called mHC, from Xie and colleagues.|It puts one rule on the mixing.|Picture four jugs pouring into four pots.
cap.n30: Every jug pours out exactly what it holds:|each column sums to 1.|Every pot ends up with exactly one jug's worth:|each row sums to 1. Nothing negative.|That is a doubly stochastic matrix.
cap.n31: And here is the trick.|Multiply two of them, and you get another one.|Her slide checks it with real numbers.
cap.n32: So stack a hundred layers,|and the total mix still obeys the rule:|the mixing itself can never stretch the signal.|Measured, the gain stays near 1.6, not 3,000.
cap.n33: With one lane, the rule leaves just the number 1:|the plain shortcut, back again.|The price is about 6.7 percent more training time,|with four lanes.|Their main test model has 27B parameters.
cap.n34: Her slide has the best picture of all this.|Attention is a person in a meeting, listening to others,|learning whose words matter more.
cap.n35: Hyper-connections are one person with four clones,|talking among themselves.|Same token, a richer picture of itself,|deeper in the network.
cap.n36: One honest limit:|the 1.8 times is counted in training tokens, on one model.|Clock time is another question.
cap.n37: So:|deep models train because every block adds onto a clean road,|and the gates stay off it.|Now the road can have lanes,|as long as every mix keeps its rows and columns at 1.
cap.n38: Next time: the knobs we set before training.
